title: The Portrait of the Bell House
premise: Ada Ravensworth, a nonbinary property surveyor, is sent to appraise Bell House, a derelict estate whose mirrors lag one second behind reality — a delay that widens each night. The house's last resident, the ancient and charming Wren Bell, cannot sign the deed until someone learns the final verse of the lullaby the house sings, because the song is the house's confession of a century-old murder it committed to protect its favorite child. Ada falls for Wren even as they realize finishing the verse will free the trapped dead and dissolve Wren along with the house; in the end Ada sings alone, choosing justice over love, and inherits only an empty lot where the mirrors once were.
about_author: Juniper Marchetti is the pen name of a former historic-building inspector who spent a decade cataloguing condemned houses across New England before turning to horror. They write about buildings that remember what people would rather forget.

chapters.title: The Lag
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Arriving at Bell House for a court-ordered appraisal, Ada notices their reflection in a hallway mirror moves a half-second late and blames exhaustion, old wiring, their own fifteen-year habit of explaining away noises. The beat is professional denial curdling into unease as the house seems to watch them take measurements.

chapters.title: Wren Bell, Last Resident
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada meets Wren, ninety-one, who refuses to sign until 'the song is finished,' and gives them a tour of rooms that rearrange when unobserved. Wren is funny, lonely, and flirtatious in a way that disarms Ada. Emotional beat: reluctant fascination — Ada came for a signature and stays for the person.

chapters.title: Verse One: What the House Wanted
chapters.summary: Ada's POV, with fragments of the house's own voice. In the nursery, Ada hears a lullaby through the walls and finds sheet music missing its last page. Researching the Bell family at the county archive, they learn a child drowned in 1923 and a servant was hanged for it. Beat: the first crack in Ada's belief in tidy explanations.

chapters.title: One Second Behind
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. The mirror delay stretches to a full second; Ada watches their reflection keep moving after they stop, and sees figures standing in reflected rooms that aren't there. When they confront Wren, Wren admits the house sings but begs them not to listen closely. Beat: fear braided with protectiveness toward Wren.

chapters.title: The Servant's Confession
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Ada in the present, the servant Maren Hale in 1923 diary entries Ada finds under floorboards. Maren didn't kill the child — she tried to save him, and the house itself drowned him to keep the family together, then let Maren hang. Beat: Ada's outrage; the theme of justice outside the law takes hold.

chapters.title: Verse Two: What the House Did
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Singing the second verse aloud makes the mirrors show 1923 live: the drowning, the trial, the noose. The dead begin appearing in reflections, mouthing words Ada can't hear. Wren grows frailer each time the song plays, aging visibly. Beat: dread plus tenderness — Ada realizes learning the song is killing Wren.

chapters.title: The Appraisal That Appraises Back
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. The house starts evaluating Ada: mirrors reflect versions of them from fifteen years ago, the night they walked away from a wrongful eviction they could have fought. The house offers a bargain — stay forever, be loved by it, never finish the song. Beat: temptation; identity theme surfaces as Ada confronts who they failed to be.

chapters.title: What Wren Knows
chapters.summary: Dual POV: Wren's memories interleaved with Ada's confrontation. Wren confesses they are the favorite child the house saved, kept alive a century past their time as long as the song stays unfinished; the missing verse is the house's admission of guilt, and singing it frees everyone — including Wren into death. Beat: love against duty made explicit; Ada must choose.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Ada's POV, climax. On the appraisal deadline, the house floods the halls with the song, trying to make Ada sing along on its terms and be absorbed. Ada finds the torn final page inside Maren's diary binding, stands in the flooded nursery, and sings the verse alone — refusing harmony, refusing the house's duet — while the dead rise through every mirror to witness. Beat: terror transfigured into resolve.

chapters.title: Empty Lot
chapters.summary: Ada's POV, resolution. The house exhales its confession, the mirrors shatter sequentially like a held breath released, and Wren dies in Ada's arms, grateful, finally one second ahead of nothing. Weeks later Ada files the report condemning the property; the county demolishes it. On the empty lot, wind carries three notes of a finished song. Beat: grief, justice served outside any courtroom, and quiet peace.
